method_card.title: Frequency Polygons, Time Series and Line Charts
method_card.content:
A frequency polygon is drawn by plotting points at the midpoint of each class and the corresponding frequency, then joining consecutive points with straight lines. The most common error — highlighted in examiner reports for this specification — is plotting at the class boundaries (start or end of the interval) rather than the midpoint.

The midpoint of a class interval is found by averaging the two boundaries: \(\text{midpoint} = \frac{\text{lower boundary} + \text{upper boundary}}{2}\). For the class 20 ≤ x < 30, the midpoint is 25. This is the x-coordinate of the plotted point; the frequency is the y-coordinate.

A time series plots a variable against time (equally spaced time points on the x-axis). Points are joined in sequence. A trend line shows the overall direction; fluctuations above and below a trend line may indicate seasonal patterns. When asked to describe a trend, include the direction (increasing/decreasing), the approximate rate of change, and any seasonal pattern visible.

A line chart is used for discrete data over time, where the intermediate values between plotted points have no meaning. This contrasts with a time series, where the data is continuous over time. Both types must have labelled axes including units.

When comparing two frequency polygons on the same axes, comment on the position (which distribution has a higher mean), the spread (which is wider), and — for Higher tier — the shape (positive/negative skew or symmetrical).
steps: Find the midpoint of each class interval: add the two boundaries and divide by 2
Join consecutive points with straight lines — do not curve or extend beyond the data
For time series, join points in time order and identify the overall trend direction
For comparisons, state a numerical comparison and interpret it in context

exam_context.marks: 2–4 marks; midpoint identification is 1 mark, reading values from a polygon is 1–2 marks, comparison-in-context is 2–4 marks
exam_context.frequency: Frequency polygons appear on most papers; the midpoint plotting error is the single most frequently penalised mistake in this topic

worked_examples.question: A grouped frequency table has classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 with frequencies 4, 9, 13, 8. What coordinate (midpoint, frequency) should be plotted for the class 10–20?

steps.label: Step 2 — Write the coordinate
steps.content: The frequency for class 10–20 is 9. The coordinate is (15, 9).

worked_examples.question: The time series below shows quarterly sales (thousands) over three years. Describe the overall trend and any seasonal pattern visible.

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify the overall trend
steps.content: The peaks (Q3 each year) rise: 15, 17, and the troughs (Q1) rise: 8, 10, 12. The overall trend is increasing.

steps.label: Step 2 — Identify the seasonal pattern
steps.content: Sales peak in Q3 (summer) each year and are lowest in Q4/Q1 (winter). There is a clear seasonal pattern repeating annually.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Overall increasing trend with a regular seasonal pattern: sales peak in Q3 and fall in Q4/Q1 each year.

worked_examples.question: Two frequency polygons for plant heights are shown below. Write a full comparison of the two distributions in context.

steps.label: Step 1 — Compare location (average)
steps.content: Group B is centred higher (peak at midpoint ~50 cm) compared with Group A (peak ~35 cm). Group B plants are taller on average.

steps.label: Step 2 — Compare spread
steps.content: Group A has a wider, flatter polygon, indicating more variation in height. Group B is narrower, so heights are more consistent.

steps.label: Step 3 — Interpret in context
steps.content: Plants grown under Condition B were typically taller (by around 15 cm) and more uniform in height, suggesting Condition B promotes more consistent growth.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Group B plants were taller on average (peak ~50 cm vs ~35 cm for A) and more consistent in height (narrower spread). Condition B promotes both greater height and more uniform growth.

bronze.display: A class interval is 40 ≤ x < 50. What is the midpoint that should be plotted on a frequency polygon?

misconceptions.message: Midpoint = (40 + 50) / 2 = 45. Never plot at 40 (the lower boundary) or 50 (the upper boundary).

bronze.display: A class interval is 15 ≤ x < 25. What is the midpoint?
The frequency polygon below shows exam scores. What is the highest frequency shown?

misconceptions.message: The highest frequency is the largest y-value on the polygon. The peak at midpoint 25 has frequency 12.

bronze.display: Which of these is the correct midpoint to plot for the class 30 ≤ x < 50 on a frequency polygon?

misconceptions.message: Midpoint = (30 + 50) / 2 = 40. Plotting at 30 or 50 is the most common error in frequency polygon questions.

bronze.display: The time series below shows monthly temperatures. Which term best describes this pattern?
options: A purely increasing trend
A seasonal pattern
A random fluctuation with no trend
A decreasing trend

misconceptions.message: The data rises and falls in a repeating annual cycle — this is a seasonal pattern, not a trend (which would be a consistent long-term direction).

bronze.display: The frequency polygon below shows student commute times. At which midpoint is the modal class?

misconceptions.message: The modal class has the highest frequency (11). Its midpoint is 25. The modal class itself would be 20–30.

bronze.display: The line chart shows monthly sales. Between which two consecutive months did sales increase by the most?
options: January to February
February to March
March to April
April to May

misconceptions.message: Changes: Jan–Feb +5, Feb–Mar +7, Mar–Apr −4, Apr–May +12. The largest increase is April to May (+12).

bronze.display: A frequency polygon represents data grouped into classes of width 10. The first midpoint plotted is at x = 5. What is the lower boundary of this first class?

misconceptions.message: Midpoint = 5, class width = 10. Lower boundary = midpoint − (width/2) = 5 − 5 = 0.

What are the midpoints (in order) that should be plotted on a frequency polygon?

misconceptions.message: Midpoints: (0+20)/2=10, (20+40)/2=30, (40+60)/2=50, (60+80)/2=70. Never use class boundaries as plotting points.

silver.display: The time series below shows quarterly revenue (£000s). Calculate the change between Q3 and Q4.

misconceptions.message: Change = Q4 − Q3 = 53 − 85 = −32 (£000). The negative sign shows a fall. Don't ignore the sign when the question asks for a change.

silver.display: Two frequency polygons are plotted below for the weights of athletes in two sports. Which comparison statement is correct in context?
options: Sport A athletes are heavier on average and more consistent in weight
Sport B athletes are heavier on average but more varied in weight
Sport A athletes are lighter but more varied; Sport B athletes are heavier and more consistent
Both sports have athletes of similar average weight

misconceptions.message: Sport B is centred higher (more mass at 85–95 kg), so heavier on average. Sport B also has a wider spread. Both comparisons need to reference the sport context.

silver.display: The frequency polygon below has a point at (35, 8) and the next point at (45, 14). Estimate the frequency at x = 40 by linear interpolation.

misconceptions.message: Halfway between midpoints 35 and 45 is 40. Halfway between frequencies 8 and 14 is (8+14)/2 = 11.

silver.display: The time series below shows annual sales for 5 years. A trend line is drawn through (Year 1, 120) and (Year 5, 162). Estimate the trend-line value at Year 3.

misconceptions.message: Trend rises from 120 to 162 over 4 intervals. Rate = (162−120)/4 = 10.5 per year. At Year 3: 120 + 2×10.5 = 141.

silver.display: The frequency polygon below shows student commute times. What is the total number of students represented?

misconceptions.message: Sum all frequencies: 3 + 10 + 16 + 8 + 3 = 40. The midpoints are x-coordinates — do not add those.

gold.display: Two frequency polygons are shown for test scores (total = 40 each). Which statement correctly compares the two distributions in context?
options: Group X scored higher on average; Group Y was more consistent
Group Y scored higher on average; Group X had more students scoring above 30
Group X scored higher on average; Group X had more students scoring above 30
Both groups had identical average scores

misconceptions.message: Group X has more frequency in the 30–50 range (10+8=18 vs 8+6=14 for Y), so Group X scored higher on average. Always check both the middle and the tails of the polygon.

gold.display: The time series below shows 8 quarters of shop sales. Calculate the first 4-point moving average.

misconceptions.message: First moving average = (45 + 60 + 72 + 50) / 4 = 227 / 4 = 56.75. Use exactly 4 consecutive values.

gold.display: Two frequency polygons for reaction times are shown. Compare the two distributions, including a comment on skewness.
options: The untrained group is centred lower (faster); the trained group is skewed towards slower times
The trained group is centred lower (faster times); the untrained group has a slight positive skew while the trained group is more symmetrical
Both distributions are symmetrical; the trained group has a higher mean
The untrained group is faster on average; both distributions are negatively skewed

misconceptions.message: Untrained peaks at 200 ms (more symmetric). Trained group peaks at 250 ms with more weight in higher times — positive skew. The trained group is actually slower on average, which is counterintuitive but matches the shifted polygon.

Estimate the number of runners aged between 35 and 55 using linear interpolation between midpoints.

misconceptions.message: 30–40 class: ages 35–40 are half the class width, so take half of 38 = 19. Class 40–50: full class = 42. Class 50–60: ages 50–55 are half the class, so half of 28 = 14. Total ≈ 19 + 42 + 14 = 75.

gold.display: The time series below shows a clear upward trend with regular Q4 dips. The trend line has equation y = 5x + 30 (x = quarter number from 1). What does the trend line predict for Quarter 12?

misconceptions.message: Substitute x = 12: y = 5(12) + 30 = 60 + 30 = 90. The trend line removes the seasonal effect — it smooths out the Q4 dips.

gold.display: A student claims that because the frequency polygon for Group A is always above Group B's polygon, Group A must have a higher mean. Is this always true?
options: Yes — a higher polygon at every point always implies a higher mean
No — if Group A is higher at low x-values and Group B is higher at high x-values, Group B could have the higher mean
No — the mean cannot be read from a frequency polygon at all
Yes — the polygon with the greater area always has the higher mean

misconceptions.message: A polygon being higher at all points means more total frequency, not necessarily a higher mean. If Group A has more frequency at lower x-values, Group B could still have the higher mean by concentrating frequency at higher x-values.
